questions.statement: You hear: "The workshop is on Friday at 3:15 p.m." What time do you note?
questions.context: A phone message for grade 11 students at a high school in Heredia gives workshop details.

options.feedback: The speaker says fifteen and stresses the minutes, so 3:15 is the time the listening part wants you to write.
This reads fifty, not fifteen. In the message the stress falls on fifteen, so the fifty version is a listening slip.
The hour is three, not five. Only the minutes are fifteen, so changing the hour misreports the announcement.
This reads forty-five. The message says fifteen, and changing the tens digit would move the workshop in the day.

questions.explanation:
Numbers ending in fifteen and fifty are the classic trap in the listening part: repeat the recording before you write the time.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You hear: "Remind Kevin to bring his permission slip on Monday." What is it?
questions.context: At a school in Alajuela a secretary leaves a short message for the parent of a student.

options.text: an invitation to a school meeting
options.feedback: An invitation would name an event, a day and a place, such as coming to the school fair. None of that is said here.

options.text: an order to buy new supplies
options.feedback: An order to buy supplies would list objects and prices. This message only reminds about one paper to bring.

options.text: a reminder about a document
options.feedback: This works because the message tells someone to act before a deadline about one item, which is a reminder.

options.text: a complaint about a missing class
options.feedback: A complaint would report a problem such as a cancelled class. This message reports nothing wrong with the school.

questions.explanation:
In the listening part, remind plus an item and a deadline signals a reminder, while an invitation names an event and an order names goods.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which opening suits a formal email to a scholarship coordinator?
questions.context: Ana writes to the scholarship coordinator of a high school in Alajuela.

options.text: Hi, I really need the money for my fees, please.
options.feedback: Hi and the phrase I really need are informal and demanding. A formal request opens with Dear plus a title and a surname.

options.text: Dear Ms. Alvarado, I am writing to ask about the scholarship.
options.feedback: This works because Dear plus a title and surname opens formally, and I am writing to ask about gives the purpose at once.

options.text: Hey lady, send me the forms as soon as possible.
options.feedback: Hey lady is slang for an unknown receiver, and send me sounds like an order rather than a request to a school office.

options.text: Dear team, what is up with the scholarship thing?
options.feedback: Dear team is not used for one named coordinator, and the question is vague, so the office cannot tell what she needs.

questions.explanation:
A formal request email opens with Dear plus the reader's title and surname, then states the reason for writing in the first sentence.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You hear: "Bring your own calculator on Friday." Which reply is correct?
questions.context: A recorded announcement at a school in Cartago gives instructions for Friday.

options.text: I will bring your calculator on Friday.
options.feedback: Your calculator would point to the calculator of the person speaking, but students were told to bring their own.

options.text: I brought my calculator on Friday.
options.feedback: Past simple suggests a finished action, yet the announcement was about a future Friday. Use will or the present simple.

options.text: My calculator is bring on Friday.
options.feedback: Is bring mixes the passive with an active verb and adds an extra ending, so this is not a possible English sentence.

options.text: I will bring my calculator on Friday, as announced.
options.feedback: This works because it answers the instruction, keeps the first person pronoun and uses will for the planned action.

questions.explanation:
To answer an announcement, echo the key noun with the right possessive and keep the future tense that the instruction implies.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which closing suits a formal email that asks the office for help?
questions.context: Ana is closing a formal email that asks the school office about a lost student card.

options.text: Thank you for your time and consideration. Yours sincerely, Ana
options.feedback: This works because the sentence thanks the reader politely and Yours sincerely is the formal close used with a named reader.

options.text: Write me soon. Bye, Ana
options.feedback: Write me soon is an order and Bye is a casual goodbye. Neither of them fits a formal email to a school office.

options.text: I do not care what you think, thanks. Ana
options.feedback: The first sentence is rude and attacks the reader, so the thanks that follows it cannot repair the tone of the email.

options.text: Let us meet at the corner at five. See you, Ana
options.feedback: Let us meet proposes an arrangement and See you is for friends, so this ending ignores the formal request that was made.

questions.explanation:
A formal letter closes with a polite sentence of thanks, then the closing phrase, then the signature written below them.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence makes the most polite request in a formal email?
questions.context: A student emails the admissions office of the University of Costa Rica.

options.text: Send me the enrollment form right now.
options.feedback: Send me at the start of a sentence is the imperative, which sounds like an order and is too direct for a first email.

options.text: Could you send me the enrollment form by Friday, please?
options.feedback: This works because Could plus you softens the demand, and placing please at the end keeps the tone formal.

options.text: You must send me the enrollment form by Friday.
options.feedback: You must is an obligation modal used from the speaker's side, so it imposes a demand instead of asking a favour.

options.text: I would like that you send me the enrollment form.
options.feedback: Would like is followed by a to-infinitive and not by that plus a clause, so this structure is ungrammatical.

questions.explanation:
In formal requests Could you or Would it be possible to softens the demand, while must and the bare imperative sound like orders.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which phrase must NOT appear in the formal email of the mock exam?
questions.context: A formal email to a school coordinator has to stay respectful, clear and polite.

options.text: Thank you for your attention.
options.feedback: Thank you for your attention is a standard formal courtesy that shows respect to a teacher or a school office.

options.text: Looking forward to hearing from you.
options.feedback: This is a standard formal close. It shows the writer expects an answer and keeps a polite distance from the reader.

options.text: I would appreciate your help.
options.feedback: Would is more formal than want in this context, and the phrase asks for help without sounding demanding at all.

options.text: Hey, thanks a lot, that would be awesome.
options.feedback: Hey, thanks a lot and awesome are informal and chatty, so they break the formal register the writing paper requires.

questions.explanation:
Register is the level of formality kept from the first line to the last, so slang such as awesome or hey must stay out of a formal email.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Who is the recorded message intended for?
questions.context: In the listening section a janitor leaves a message on the answerphone of a school in Escazu.

options.text: The student who lost a locker key
options.feedback: This works because the message names the locker and the key, so the only person concerned is the student who lost it.

options.text: The driver of the school bus
options.feedback: No bus, route or stop is mentioned anywhere, so the driver is not the person the caller is trying to reach.

options.text: The librarian who orders the books
options.feedback: An order of books would appear in the message if the librarian were the target, but no book or order is named.

options.text: The cook of the school cafeteria
options.feedback: The cafeteria is never mentioned, and a lost locker key has nothing to do with meals or with kitchen work.

questions.explanation:
Identify the audience by scanning for the object named in the message: a locker key points to the student, not to the school staff.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which order of parts suits a formal complaint email?
questions.context: Marcos lost his lab coat at the technical school in Escazu and writes to the coordinator.

options.text: Problem, greeting, closing, request
options.feedback: The greeting must open the email and the closing must end it. This version hides the greeting and stops without a proper ending.

options.text: Greeting, request, problem, closing
options.feedback: Asking for something before explaining the loss confuses the reader, who does not yet know what happened to the coat.

options.text: Greeting, problem, request, closing
options.feedback: This works because the email opens formally, describes the problem, states what she wants and only then closes politely.

options.text: Closing, greeting, problem, request
options.feedback: Starting with the closing makes the text unreadable, since the reader gets no greeting and no idea of the complaint.

questions.explanation:
A formal complaint follows a fixed order: greeting, useful context, description of the problem, request, thanks and closing.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She says: "I have called twice and nobody answered." How does she sound?
questions.context: A mother phones the school in Tibas after calling twice and nobody has answered.

options.text: calm and completely relaxed
options.feedback: Repeating the number of calls signals annoyance. A relaxed speaker would not stress that she has phoned twice already.

options.text: irritated but still polite
options.feedback: This works because the flat tone plus the repeated detail I have called twice show controlled irritation and no insults.

options.text: excited about the new school term
options.feedback: Nothing in the sentence expresses excitement about a term, and the complaint clearly shows the opposite feeling.

options.text: confused about which class to attend
options.feedback: Confusion about a class would ask which class or when it starts. She is complaining about not getting an answer at all.

questions.explanation:
Speakers show irritation with repeated details, overlong flat sentences and emphatic stress rather than with rude language.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence rewrites the informal note in formal English?
questions.context: A short note to a friend asks for the bus timetable in very casual language.

options.text: Can you send me the bus timetable, huh?
options.feedback: huh is informal filler and Can is less polite than Could, so the tone does not change enough for a formal email.

options.text: Send me the bus timetable, ok?
options.feedback: ok at the end is casual, and the bare imperative between friends sounds like an order in a letter to a school.

options.text: Could you send me the bus timetable, please?
options.feedback: This works because Could plus you and please soften the demand, and timetable is the formal word for a bus schedule.

options.text: You will send me the bus timetable now.
options.feedback: You will and now form a command stated as a fact, so the sentence demands the action instead of requesting it politely.

questions.explanation:
To raise the register, replace the bare imperative with Could you, drop fillers such as huh or ok and choose formal nouns.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Who offers to pay for part of the class trip?
questions.context: Two speakers discuss a class trip: a teacher and a parent talking on the phone.

options.text: The teacher, who works at the school
options.feedback: This works because the offer comes from inside the school, so the teacher is the speaker who proposes paying a share.

options.text: The parent, who calls during the message
options.feedback: The parent asks about the cost, so she is the listener collecting information and not the one offering money.

options.text: The student, who answers the door
options.feedback: No student speaks in this message. The proposal is made between the school and the family, so she cannot be the speaker.

options.text: The driver, who waits in the van
options.feedback: The driver is never heard, and the conversation is only about payment, so he cannot be the one who makes the offer.

questions.explanation:
To track the speakers, note the vocabulary each one uses: offering a payment signals the speaker inside the school, asking signals the caller.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence has the wrong tense for a formal complaint?
questions.context: A student complains to the coordinator about a scholarship answer sent in June.

options.text: I wrote to the office last Monday.
options.feedback: Past simple is correct here because last Monday fixes a finished moment in the past before the complaint was written.

options.text: They have not answered me yet.
options.feedback: Present perfect with not yet is correct, since the answering started in the past and still has not happened.

options.text: I am writing to ask about the scholarship.
options.feedback: Present simple is standard in the opening line of a formal email, because the act of writing takes place now.

options.text: I received your email yesterday and I still wait for an answer.
options.feedback: This is the wrong one: still wait describes an unfinished situation now, so it needs the present continuous form.

questions.explanation:
An unfinished state takes the present continuous (I am still waiting); the present simple wrongly suggests a completed action.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: You hear: "The mock exam is on the 16th of April." Which date do you write?
questions.context: A school secretary reads the exam dates aloud in a noisy corridor in Cartago.

options.text: April 6
options.feedback: Sixteen keeps the silent ending that the speaker pronounces. Dropping it turns the date into a completely different day.

options.text: April 16
options.feedback: This works because sixteen ends in -teen and the speaker adds the month, so the note is April 16.

options.text: April 26
options.feedback: Twenty-six begins with twenty, which sounds nothing like sixteen, so the day of the exam has been misheard.

options.text: April 10
options.feedback: Ten is one stressed syllable like six, but sixteen has two syllables and a silent t that the speaker keeps.

questions.explanation:
Listen for the -teen and -ty endings: sixteen, seventeen and eighteen all keep a silent t that the speaker never releases.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which opening states the purpose of the email in the clearest way?
questions.context: Luis applies for an exchange semester at a school in Madrid, Spain.

options.text: Hello, my name is Luis and I am sixteen years old.
options.feedback: Giving your name and age adds background. A formal email should state the reason for writing in its very first line.

options.text: It is very hot here and we have no snow at all.
options.feedback: Talking about heat and snow describes Costa Rica instead of the request, so the office learns nothing about the purpose.

options.text: I am writing to apply for the exchange semester in Spain.
options.feedback: This works because I am writing to apply for plus the programme name gives the aim and the subject in one line.

options.text: Everybody says your programme is the best in Central America.
options.feedback: This is only an opinion about the programme. It is not a request and it asks the reader for no action at all.

questions.explanation:
Put the goal first with a purpose phrase such as I am writing to apply for, and only then add the supporting details.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which note records every detail the listening part asks for?
questions.context: The listening part of the mock exam asks for the date, the time and the item to bring.

options.text: Sat 8 June, bring ID card and receipt
options.feedback: The time is missing, so the student would lose the mark for that detail even though the day and the items are correct.

options.text: 10 a.m., bring ID card and receipt
options.feedback: Only the time and the items were noted down. The date is the first detail the exam asks the listener to write.

options.text: Sat 8 June, 10 a.m., meet at the office
options.feedback: The day and the time are right, but meet at the office changes the item, because nobody said to meet there.

options.text: Sat 8 June, 10 a.m., bring ID card and receipt
options.feedback: This works because it holds the date, the time and both items, which are exactly the details the question requires.

questions.explanation:
Note-taking tasks score one point per detail, so write the date, the time and each item separately instead of guessing them.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which question asks the school office about the mock exam results?
questions.context: In the writing part a student must ask the school office about the mock exam results.

options.text: How much was the exam?
options.feedback: How much asks about a price or a quantity, and the exam results are information to be given, not money to be paid.

options.text: When are we going to know the exam results?
options.feedback: This works because When plus are plus the subject builds a complete question, and to know keeps the future meaning.

options.text: How long the exam was?
options.feedback: How long needs a subject and a verb after it, as in How long the exam was. A real question requires the auxiliary.

options.text: How many the exam results are?
options.feedback: How many expects a countable noun, but results goes with know here, so both the preposition and the word order fail.

questions.explanation:
A question word comes first, then the auxiliary or the verb be, then the subject: When are we going to know the results?

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which ending is correct for a formal request email?
questions.context: Ana closes an email to the school after asking for a replacement student card.

options.text: Yours sincerely, thank you for your help, Ana
options.feedback: Yours sincerely belongs on the last line, and a closing phrase cannot be joined by commas into a single sentence.

options.text: Thank you for your help. See you soon, Ana
options.feedback: See you soon is for friends, so it breaks the formal register required after a request to a school office.

options.text: Thank you for your help. I look forward to your reply. Yours sincerely, Ana
options.feedback: This works because it gives the thanks, then the sentence about the reply, then the closing and the name, in that order.

options.text: Hello Ana, thank you, bye
options.feedback: Hello and bye belong to a chat between friends, and no formal closing phrase appears for a named reader such as a coordinator.

questions.explanation:
End in this order: a sentence of thanks, a sentence about the expected reply, the closing phrase, then your full name below.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which sentence should the email use after that message?
questions.context: You hear the school coordinator move the field trip from Tuesday to Friday, 14 November.

options.text: Thank you for the new date, Friday 14 November.
options.feedback: This works because it thanks the coordinator, repeats the new date she gave and keeps the formal you in the right order.

options.text: Thank you for the new date, Friday 4 November.
options.feedback: The message said the fourteenth and not the fourth, so writing 4 November reports a date that nobody announced.

options.text: I moved the trip to Friday 4 November myself.
options.feedback: I moved says the writer did it, but the coordinator changed it, so the agent in the message has been swapped.

options.text: You moved our trip to Friday, so thanks a lot.
options.feedback: You moved names the wrong agent for the change, and thanks a lot is far too informal for an email to a member of staff.

questions.explanation:
After a phone message, confirm the exact detail you heard, keep the person who made the change as the subject and stay formal.

questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which email is complete and correct for the mock exam task?
questions.context: A grade 11 student in Monteverde must write one complete formal email for the mock exam.

options.text: Hey! Send me the syllabus now or I will fail. Bye
options.feedback: It has no formal greeting and no closing, and it threatens the teacher, so it would lose marks on register and on tone.

options.text: Dear Ms. Rojas, I am writing to ask about the trip. Ana
options.feedback: The greeting and the purpose are fine, but the email never says what she wants, so the request itself is missing.

options.text: Dear Ms. Rojas, could you send me the syllabus, please? Ana
options.feedback: The polite request is good, but the email stops after Ana with no closing phrase and no line thanking the reader.

options.text: Dear Ms. Rojas, I am writing to ask about the trip to Monteverde. Could you send me the syllabus? Thank you. Yours sincerely, Ana Perez
options.feedback: This works because it has the greeting, the purpose, a polite request, a thank you, the closing and the full name.

questions.explanation:
Marks are given for the four parts together: formal greeting, clear purpose, polite request and a proper closing with the signature.
